title: Why Heat Pumps are Essential for the Future - Explained
summary: Undecided explains air-source and ground-source heat pumps, their efficiency, cold-weather limits, upfront costs and savings by fuel, plus heat pump water heaters and dryers.

assertions.quote: it’s not creating heat energy it’s only moving it
When the ambient temperature drops to -10ºC (about 14ºF) or lower, the heat pump's electric power consumption rate increases
at very low temperatures, frost can accumulate over the outdoor coil, which can reduce efficiency

verdicts.note: Frost on the outdoor coil restricts airflow, and defrost cycles reverse the refrigeration cycle, using energy, reducing heat pump availability and increasing auxiliary heating; the humidity dependence is not tested here.
Defrost cut ccASHP COP at site 2 (e.g. 1.86 to 1.65 at 10-20F), drove backup energy use between the 10F changeover and 40F, and eliminating it would have raised annual energy savings by 8.3%.
Defrost consumed over 20% of compressor heating energy at Sites 5, 7, 8 and 11; defrost cycles peaked at 20-40F wet-bulb, since cold air holds little moisture.

Site conditions caused long defrost periods that lowered efficiency, and at one windy oceanfront site prolonged defrost cycles pulled heat out of the house; this is anecdotal plus the evaluators' general observation.

Frost on the outdoor coil in cold humid air cuts heat exchange, and the reverse-cycle defrost pulls heat from the house and drops supply air temperature; defrost took a median 5-8% of energy at 5-35 F and up to 16% of the time at one site.

assertions.quote: if you consider a natural gas boiler, the savings are lower since gas is so cheap
the savings depend on the location and climate of the installation

verdicts.note: Bill savings vary by climate, prices and housing stock across locations, and vary even more between the 5th and 95th percentiles within one location.
Adoption economics vary by grid region, climate, housing and especially baseline heating fuel: gas rarely pays, resistance almost always does.
Edwards finds bill benefits vary across the US, with the primary heating fuel a key driver and climate and energy prices also important.
RMI's lifetime cost results flip with fuel (propane and oil favour heat pumps), with whether an AC is replaced too, with new build versus retrofit, and with city climate and prices.
Simple payback ranged from 0.6 years (furnace and AC both failed) to 28.8 years (no failure, versus a condensing furnace), depending on what equipment is replaced and the baseline furnace efficiency.

Cost-competitiveness varies most with regional energy prices and climate: heat pumps win even under worst-case assumptions in Montreal, Halifax and Vancouver but not in cold, cheap-gas Edmonton; the replaced equipment is not varied.

assertions.quote: their problem is the high upfront cost

verdicts.note: Ground-source heat pumps offer greater efficiency and cold-climate performance than air-source but are an even more expensive solution; stated, not analysed.

RMI notes that ground-source heat pumps use less energy on the coldest days because ground temperature stays moderate, but have historically cost significantly more than air-source because of drilling.

LBNL: ground-source heat pumps were the most expensive type, at nearly three times the total system cost of ductless and ducted air-source systems; the report does not test the 'run cheaper' half of the claim.
Ground-source heat pumps are highly efficient but more complex and expensive to install because of drilling; running costs are not quantified and they are left out of the model.

assertions.quote: they have a payback period of 5-10 years

verdicts.note: DOE's 5-10 year figure assumes favourable fuels and incentives; against gas without credits paybacks are often much longer.

assertions.quote: can work efficiently basically everywhere since the ground has lower temperature variations

verdicts.note: Ground temperatures a few metres down stay near the annual mean, so ground-source COP varies little with weather.
RMI explains that ground-source heat pumps suit cold climates because the ground stays moderate when the air is very cold, so they use less energy on the coldest days.
Ground-source heat pumps draw heat from below ground, are highly efficient and perform well in extreme temperatures (a descriptive secondary citation).
